newsitem.title: NORWAY: NATO ministers to discuss Bosnia, expansion in Norway.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers to discuss Bosnia, expansion in Norway.

text.p: NATO defence ministers gathered in Norway on Tuesday for a two-day meeting that will focus on keeping the peace in post-war Bosnia as well as ponder the Western alliance's eastward expansion.

The informal talks, which begin on Wednesday, will give the 16 ministers their first chance after the Bosnian elections to discuss what follow-on force to keep in the war-torn country after the current mission's mandate ends in December.

The ministers will also get an opportunity to meet new Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who on Thursday will sign an agreement with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry and Norwegian Defence Minister Joergen Kosmo on tackling Russian military pollution in the Arctic.
"I have never met my new Russian colleague," Kosmo told the Norwegian news agency NTB. "I understand he is a reflecting person who thinks carefully before speaking his mind."
Norwegian officials said Bosnia was first on the agenda in the NATO talks in a closely guarded hotel in the picturesque west coast town of Bergen.

Western allies accept that a force will have to stay to prevent conflict and give last year's Dayton peace accords time to take root, but its size, make-up and mandate have yet to be agreed. The issue is sensitive in the United States where presidential elections take place on November 5.

President Bill Clinton originally promised that U.S. troops would be in Bosnia no longer than the current mandate for the 55,000-strong force. But America's main European allies have made clear they will not stay without a U.S. troop commitment.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has said the alliance would have to remain engaged beyond the end of the year, probably with a smaller force including U.S. troops.

Elections on September 14 underlined Bosnia's ethnic divide and highlighted the problems ahead in trying to create the common institutions foreseen in Dayton to reunify the country. Even with NATO mounting a big security operation, few refugees took the risk of crossing ethnic boundaries to vote in their former homes.
Former Warsaw Pact states, such as Poland and Hungary, want to remain and see close cooperation in the new force as a way of strengthening their case for NATO membership next year.
NATO's expansion, a highly touchy issue for the Russians, will be discussed on Thursday morning before the ministers go into a so-called 16+1 meeting with Rodionov, officials said.

Earlier on Tuesday, NATO defence ministers meeting ex-Warsaw Pact and non-aligned officials in Copenhagen sought to encourage the former Soviet Baltic republics in their bid for membership while reassuring Russia that an enlarged alliance was no threat.

In a speech prepared for delivery to a closed-door seminar on Baltic Sea regional security, German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said eastern European countries not immediately able to join NATO must not feel rejected.
"Neither NATO nor the European Union can take in all countries who wish to become members at the same time. But the door will remain open to those who cannot join with the first wave," he said.
Although a firm decision on new members is not expected before a NATO summit early next year, Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are widely seen as the most immediate candidates.
